body_markdown:
Ford GTs. Plymouth Cudas. A Porsche 911 GT3 RS. And the thing that nearly broke me, a three-wheeled Honda ATC200X that rolled onto the auction block during the first day of last weekend’s Barrett-Jackson auction in Las Vegas. The event was at times a car auction, a three-ring circus, and a reality show. It’s (mostly) a well-oiled machine.


Hagerty recently partnered with Barrett-Jackson, and as part of the deal, I work with the broadcast crew in various capacities. That access gave me a behind-the-curtain view of what this organization pulls off—and I came away genuinely impressed.


But first, the market. What Barrett-Jackson really is, stripped of the spectacle, is pure commerce in its most transparent form. A product rolls up, a crowd decides what it’s worth, and a gavel falls. No negotiating, no posturing, no wondering if the dealer is playing you. The market speaks and it speaks fast. If you know how to inspect a car—really inspect it—there may be no more efficient way to buy one. The price is the price, and it’s set by everyone in the room simultaneously.


The risk is the same as the reward. You have minutes, not days. No cooling-off period. Buy wrong and you own it anyway. Barrett-Jackson sells the vast majority of its cars with no reserve—the crowd’s judgment is the only judgment that matters. A small number of high-value cars carry a reserve, but they are the exception, not the rule.


Barrett-Jackson


The range of what crosses that block is genuinely staggering. Last weekend in Las Vegas the same gavel that fell on Bentley Continental GTs and rows of immaculate restomods also fell on[a custom stretched limousine with a massive joint attached to its roof](https://www.barrett-jackson.com/2026-las-vegas/docket/vehicle/2001-ford-excursion-custom-limousine-300573?origin=results) ($10,120), a[Mad Max fever dream](https://www.barrett-jackson.com/2026-las-vegas/docket/vehicle/1972-chevrolet-chevelle-custom-coupe-302527) of a car that looked like it drove in from the apocalypse ($18,700), and[the Mystery Machine](https://www.barrett-jackson.com/2026-las-vegas/docket/vehicle/1994-gmc-vandura-mystery-machine-re-creation-302443?origin=results) —yes, *that* Mystery Machine, Scooby-Doo’s van rendered in metal and paint ($20,900). VW Microbuses sat alongside six-figure muscle cars. The auction does not curate for taste. It curates for desire, and desire turns out to be a very broad category.


What drives the crowd is something harder to quantify than horsepower or provenance. Some of it is nostalgia—I mowed countless lawns as a kid to save up for an ATC200X, and when[that tricycle](https://www.barrett-jackson.com/2026-las-vegas/docket/vehicle/1986-honda-atc-200x-three-wheeler-302733?origin=results) rolled across the block, the excitement I felt as a teenager rushed over me. That’s a powerful drug. But nostalgia only explains part of the room. Plenty of bidders simply want a beautiful object, a new toy, something that makes the neighbors slow down as they drive past. The motivations are as varied as the cars themselves. What Barrett-Jackson does brilliantly is put all of those motivations in the same room at the same time and point them at the same gavel.


Barrett-Jackson has been doing this since 1971, when Russ Jackson and Tom Barrett started the auction in Scottsdale, Arizona. Craig Jackson now runs it as chairman and CEO, and he is everywhere. I watched him personally direct the broadcast crew for the weekend’s charity auction—when UFC president Dana White took the stage to present two trucks that were being sold for charity.


One of the trucks was the first production version of the new[Ram Rumble Bee SRT](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/ram-goes-full-send-with-rumble-bee-sport-trucks/) . The entire hammer price went to the Folds of Honor and the UFC foundation. Since it was the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, the crowd was especially tuned in. Jackson knew exactly what the moment required and managed it like a conductor. The bidding included Dana White himself; he eventually triumphed with a $1.5 million bid.


Later a man dressed as Batman joined a couple of cars onstage to, I guess, generate interest and hawk the cars. That felt about right for Las Vegas. And yet somehow, amid the joint limo and the Mystery Machine and the caped crusader working the crowd, the whole thing ran with the precision of a live network broadcast—because that is exactly what it is.


Brandan Gillogly


Behind the spectacle is a production that runs nearly eight hours a day across three days, moving some 600 vehicles through a single auction block without losing the thread. Announcers who never lose their voice or their energy. Porters who move cars on and off the block with military precision. Camera operators who anticipate the moment before it happens. Directors calling shots in real time with no script to fall back on. Every car has a story. Every bidder has a number. Every moment is live. The people who pull this off do so through sheer experience—they have done it enough times that the chaos looks like choreography. From where I was standing, it was one of the more impressive live productions I have seen.


If my experience last weekend puts you in a shopping mood, I encourage you to look at Hagerty Marketplace, where there are now some 1000 cars available. Wow. Here are a few of my favorites.


- [A 1990 Jeep Grand Wagoneer with only 59K miles.](https://www.hagerty.com/marketplace/auction/1990-Jeep-Wagoneer/1be47b8a-8c80-4107-bff0-39b9141ae6a3)
- [This 1974 Jensen Interceptor had one owner for decades.](https://www.hagerty.com/marketplace/auction/1974-Jensen-Interceptor/d2d7fca1-4614-4250-8f82-e1c6d1d404fa)
- [This super clean example of Datsun’s revolutionary 240Z.](https://www.hagerty.com/marketplace/auction/1971-Datsun-240Z/09c093d8-59ea-45ce-9938-5ff782b275d8)
- [A one-family-owned 1981 Corvette in a fetching color.](https://www.hagerty.com/marketplace/auction/1981-Chevrolet-Corvette/aa4504de-393f-4fc7-ab2f-5785fae1e3f7)


I’ll be on assignment next week so this newsletter will take a break. In the meantime:


Never Stop Driving!


Larry
